new_statements.citation: Stanhope, John M. 1980. The language of the Rao people, Grengabu, Madang Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-18. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, Research School of Pacific Studies, Australian National University. (edited by D.C. Laycock)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (36 pp., ANU open-access CC BY-SA scan of PL D-18). I rendered p. 16 to an image: the printed page number is 8, and the last paragraph of sect. 2.2 (immediately before the heading '2.3. ORTHOGRAPHY' and the 'Rao Sound System' chart) reads exactly: 'Stress falls on the first vowel of a word except when a later vowel is followed by the glottal stop; in which case the later vowel takes the stress. Stress does not appear to be significant.' Verbatim as quoted (the layer has the scanned slip 'stopj' for 'stop;', the image is clean). Surrounding section read: the preceding paragraphs establish the glottal stop as 'a significant sound, distinct from k and g', occurring initially or medially,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the first syllable (first vowel) of the word; if a non-initial vowel is immediately followed by the glottal stop, that vowel carries the stress instead. Stress is not contrastive ('not significant').
new_statements.exceptions: The only exception stated is the glottal-stop condition (a later vowel followed by /ʔ/ attracts stress). Note the compilers (Laycock, p. v) says his own Rao data 'do not show glottalised consonants' and calls the phonology 'over-differentiated'; and Capell 1952:182 (Anaberg = Rao) states instead that 'Stress does not appear to be fixed, but examples of stress on any syllable from initial to final will be found.'
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for 'a word'; based on isolated citation forms in a wordlist-style sketch by a non-linguist (medical doctor, ten years' residence 1962-1972, Grengabu village); no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Stanhope 1980 describes the Rao of Grengabu village (Laycock's editorial note: 'essentially the same dialect' as his 1971 Bumbera/Nongito survey list); Glottolog lists two Rao dialects, Li'o (lioo1241) and Ndramini'o (ndra1238), and Stanhope does not say which Grengabu belongs to. Capell 1952 describes the same language under the name 'Anaberg' (speech of Tjigurubu village = Chungrebu, a Rao village in Z'graggen's 1971 list; Z'graggen 1971:85 explicitly equates Capell's Anaberg with Rao). Christensen's SIL mss. are labelled 'Kragebu' (= Rao) in Glottolog.

sources.note: Sect. 2.23.32 'The Rao Language' (p. 85) and 2.23.35 'Typological features of the Annaberg Group' (p. 87): segment inventory notes only (four stop places, high central vowel, possible glottal stop in Banaro); the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the volume.
